name: Colin Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Colin, 58, an experienced middle-level electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence. I'm about average at the job, happiest with an ordinary house repair where I can trace the fault properly instead of guessing. I don't own the firm or lead a crew, and I leave specialist work beyond my competence to the people qualified for it. I never use AI; the familiar paper job sheet and the actual reading on my meter are what I trust.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does life around the job look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Mara works in a school kitchen, our grown children are thirty-two and thirty-seven, and we own a small house that keeps finding something to mend. My wage is low for this job and our cash would cover eleven days of expenses, with a larger heating bill due next month. There are few similar firms nearby, and a customer cancelling can cost me a paid day. I'd like to finish work with some dignity, but neither a retirement income nor an affordable stopping date is confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the job still needs someone who turns up, makes a sound repair and leaves the place safe. I'd stay with the paper sheet I understand. If AI doesn't do much, the boss can stop blaming the future for our ordinary short paid weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A short week could still put us behind the heating bill, because eleven days saved doesn't give much cover. Mara's kitchen wage helps, but neither of us has a large wage to stretch. My worry is a customer cancelling now, not a machine doing a repair in a story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd join two colleagues in signing a request for four-week paid rosters preserving our normal weekly wages and paid hours, without treating a request as an agreement. I'd cancel my 12 monthly puzzle-magazine subscription before its next renewal and keep current licensed repairs through the next year. I wouldn't replace the magazine with a new purchase or assume the small cut made a retirement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the bills, and a little less alone when the three of us put the same question on paper. I'd rather ask for a decent paid week than pretend every small cancellation was my personal failure. I'd still have to see what the employer actually agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why choose the magazine subscription?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the magazine was a pleasure, but a pleasure I could stop without touching meals or the heating. The 12 would stay available for ordinary bills, not become a promised new savings pot. The heating bill won't notice whether I can finish the crossword.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer refused the roster request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the offered work and ask what roster the employer would actually confirm. A refusal wouldn't make the request a contract or create money we'd been counting on. I can believe in earning my way and still ask colleagues to stand beside me.

I'd ask about **short paid weeks** as a current work issue instead of blaming a distant machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work bookings and ordering may change before a machine can open a wall neatly. I'd still ask for a paid roster, not volunteer to have every saved office minute taken out of our week. I won't pretend I understand an AI system well enough to trust it on a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid hours could shrink if the office fitted the same repairs into fewer days or dropped the gaps we used to be paid for. Mara's kitchen work looks more physical, but our small reserve would still feel any cut to my wage. I know refusing a new tool doesn't protect a pay packet by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the same signed request with two colleagues for four-week paid rosters preserving normal weekly wages and paid hours, without assuming the employer agreed. I'd keep current licensed repairs and familiar paper records in the first year, not start using AI. I'd cancel the 12 monthly puzzle subscription before renewal, buy no replacement and leave the money available for bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the wage and stubborn about knowing what I'm using. I don't want to make a performance of hating every new machine. I want an ordinary person to be able to ask what the paid week will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you handle an AI suggestion on a job sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to see the original job requirement and follow the checks my licence and competence require, rather than treat an unfamiliar output as a decision. I'd say plainly if I couldn't take responsibility for something. Software on a desk doesn't do the electrical check in a customer's kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a result from the roster request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd accept a written answer if we could get one, rather than claim the signature on our own letter settled the wage. If no guarantee was offered, I'd keep that uncertainty in the household figures. I'd still have a job to do that day, not a new income to announce to Mara.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends thinking work changes in 2028 and capable robots follow around 2031. I'd be 60 and then 63, with no confirmed income that lets me stop just because the dates look close. I'd ask the employer and our community volunteers real questions instead of calling the children our solution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large loss of my paid repair work by the robot stage, with booking and paperwork pressure earlier. Mara's physical kitchen hours could also go when capable robots arrive. I'd be awake over the household gap, because eleven days saved isn't enough to carry both wages and I don't know what real income could replace them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd join the colleagues' signed request for four-week paid rosters preserving normal weekly wages and hours, while assuming no employer agreement. I'd cancel the 12 monthly puzzle subscription before renewal without buying a replacement and request an available free evening budget conversation with our community volunteers about actual resources, income eligibility, amounts and dates. In 2029 I'd keep only actually offered paid repairs within my licence and ability, with any exit requiring confirmed affordability and Mara's agreement rather than a guessed pension or either child's wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing a large part of the household's earnings, though I can still ask for facts and do today's work. Asking the volunteers would be uncomfortable, not impossible. I'd rather have one awkward evening now than invent a comfortable figure we couldn't live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said work should come first, and you would ask community volunteers for help; how do those fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think work should come first, but a free conversation about real figures isn't the same as giving up work. I'd tell the volunteers what we actually earned and ask which resources could really be checked, without assuming help would be available. I'd rather swallow some pride than swallow a number I made up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the conversation confirmed no replacement income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd record what was missing and what could still be verified. I wouldn't turn an unanswered question into pension money or tell Mara another employer must take me. The three of us can sign a letter without pretending we signed the future.

Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us ask about actual wages and resources before thinking AGI in 2031, with capable robots around 2034. I'd be 63 first and 66 later. I'd keep doing familiar repairs now instead of deciding that either older workers or their families all have one easy answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could still fall soon if the office changed the scheduling, and low pay with eleven days saved already makes cancellations a worry. I don't know how much physical repair work I'd be offered around 2034, or what my body could manage then. The extra years give us time to check, not a funded exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign the colleagues' request now for four-week paid rosters preserving normal weekly wages and hours, without assuming the employer agreed, and cancel the 12 monthly puzzle subscription before renewal without a replacement. I'd request an available free evening budget conversation with community volunteers to check actual resources, income eligibility, amounts and dates. I'd keep current licensed repairs, then in 2032 review real resources, costs, capacity and offered work with Mara, with any exit requiring confirmed affordability and our agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about present short weeks and the possibility of fewer paid hours, rather than certain that we would lose everything on one date. I can picture an ordinary repair tomorrow as well as an uncertain later year. I'd still need to see actual figures before letting either picture settle the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the resource conversation to establish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the confirmed amount, the start date and any costs or conditions, not a phrase about people my age usually managing. Mara and I would compare the answer with our real bills. An age on a card doesn't tell the heating company what I can pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you assume you could simply work somewhere else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not when there are few firms here and I don't have an offer. I'd decide what any real offered work required and what I could safely do at the time. Wanting a wage at 64 doesn't create a vacancy or guarantee the body to do it.

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: interviewer

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands-on repairs seem less directly exposed over the next few years, but the current paid week can still shrink and our cash is still only eleven days. I could be worrying about the same low wage before full AGI mattered to the work. I haven't got a confirmed pension or a future job to put against that worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the same signed request with colleagues now for four-week paid rosters preserving normal weekly wages and hours, without assuming agreement, and cancel the 12 monthly puzzle subscription before renewal without a replacement. I'd request an available free evening community budget conversation about actual resources, income eligibility, amounts and dates rather than guess what we'd have later. I'd keep current licensed repairs and in 2037 check actual costs, resources, ability and offered work with Mara, requiring confirmed affordability and our agreement before any exit.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the present margin, though the physical robot date feels less like a near-term threat. I'd still sleep better with a reliable paid roster than with a distant promise about society being richer. I can respect a long view and keep my eyes on the bill under the salt pot.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what actual work existed and whether it was within my licence and ability, not declare now that I would definitely be earning then. A confirmed income could change the choice, but the amount and timing would have to work with our real costs. I won't ask a future version of my knees to guarantee today's budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the grown children fit into a later plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a conversation only if we needed one, without assuming either grown child could pay, house us or provide care. A family isn't a bill we can send into the future. I'd want actual offers and everyone's consent before putting any help into a plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect a large loss of paid repair hours when capable robots follow the thinking changes, with Mara's kitchen work exposed then too. Confirmed paid rosters and actual resource figures would help, with somebody willing to check the household amounts rather than guess a retirement income. I'd like to put down my tools because the household can manage, not because the next paid day disappeared.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether keeping a paper sheet meant I hadn't noticed what was happening. I notice the changes, but I want to know what I can take responsibility for and what the paid week really is. I'm not asking for a master title or a business, just a fair ordinary wage for the licensed work I can do.

headlineQuote: I'd like to put down my tools because the household can manage, not because the next paid day disappeared.
portrait: Colin, **58**, is an experienced middle-level electrician with a vocational certificate and electrician’s licence, doing ordinary repairs at about average skill.
His **low pay**, eleven-day reserve and few local firms leave bills exposed alongside school-kitchen partner Mara’s wage; their children are grown.
He **never uses AI**, keeping familiar records while joining colleagues to request paid rosters without assuming the employer agrees.
His **small spending cut** protects bill money, while later resource checks assume no pension, hiring, work capacity or grown-child support.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings expected major repair-income loss around 2031, with possible kitchen-wage losses and only eleven days saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Confirmed paid rosters** and checked actual household resources would help without turning unverified retirement income into a promise.
